video_title: Nancy Zimmerman: People, Process, and Fixed Income Arbitrage at Bracebridge Capital
gist: Nancy Zimmerman of Bracebridge Capital explains why fixed income arbitrage inefficiencies persist, how the firm sizes positions and manages crisis risk, and why hyperscaler debt issuance and policy experimentation create today's opportunities.

insights.claim: Bracebridge's founders pitched Yale's David Swenson in 1994 on fixed income arbitrage that avoids rate-direction bets, and Swenson replied that other managers claiming to do this spent much of their risk capital and time guessing which way rates were going.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: True market-neutral fixed income arb was scarce in the 1990s, and the pure-relative-value niche has been a durable edge.

insights.claim: Fixed income inefficiencies persist for decades because of constrained agents: investor habitat, market segmentation, narrow mandates, and indexes that quickly become strategies themselves.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Structural constraints, not information gaps, create the persistent mispricings; look for forced or mandate-bound holders.
insights.quote: A lot of inefficiencies come from places where you have a constrained economic agent.

insights.claim: Ratings are positively serially correlated and backward looking, and index construction depends on them, which creates mispricing at ratings and index boundaries.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Benchmark and ratings-driven flows are a recurring source of dislocations in credit.

insights.claim: Benchmark-driven passive investing and ETFs that must create and destroy units mechanically, especially with added leverage, produce unusual second-order effects that arbitrageurs can exploit.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Passive flows add mechanical price pressure that can be traded against.

insights.claim: Newness (new instruments), changes in rate or volatility levels, and shifts in market ownership or borrowing appetite are the triggers that create fixed income opportunities.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Regime change and ownership turnover are the entry signals for relative-value hunting.

insights.claim: Zimmerman says she would have expected developed market rates to become more efficient since 1994, but opportunities persist because markets are bigger and more complex, and there are now about 48 instruments describing risk-free US rates in the first three years of the curve versus three at the start of her career.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Instrument proliferation is itself a source of arbitrage in rates.
insights.quote: If you told me in 1994 that I would still be finding opportunities in develop market rates today, I would have thought you were nuts.

insights.claim: Emerging market arbitrage persists because many investors want only a little EM and benchmark indexes hold dollar bonds, leaving out-of-index bonds, such as same-obligor bonds in other currencies, inefficiently priced once swapped back to a single currency.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Pairing dollar and local-currency bonds of the same obligor lets investors harvest EM alpha without a view on the sovereign credit.

insights.claim: Bracebridge sizes positions bottom-up and then aggregates by common driver, since many positions that look separate share one force or sector, with overarching concentration limits on how much balance sheet sits in a given market or name.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Position size should be set on correlated exposure, not on the line item.

insights.claim: Secured positions carry collateral that covaries with its sector, so collateral exposure must be counted in concentration limits, and identical arbitrages can be repriced because investors label one flavor good and another bad.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Hedged positions still carry sector and sentiment risk through collateral and category labels.

insights.claim: Bracebridge keeps diversification and liquidity to retain buying power on days when forced sellers dump assets, and distinguishes drawdown from capital impairment.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Dry powder and liquidity are the real payoff of stress testing for relative-value funds.
insights.quote: You want to think hard about what's the difference between a draw down and a capital impairment because those are different things.

insights.claim: Crises teach arbitrageurs to examine reliance on institutions, courts, banks and counterparties; in the middle of COVID Bracebridge bought Treasuries in escrow at 80 cents on the dollar.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Liquid positions let a fund move quickly into indiscriminate selling.
insights.quote: In the middle of CO, we're buying treasuries in escrow at 80 cents on the dollar.

insights.claim: Zimmerman says the opportunity set must govern fund size: Bracebridge does not 'stock the lake' and was once closed to new capital for almost a decade.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Capacity discipline in arbitrage strategies matters, and heavy QE periods leave little to do.
insights.quote: We don't stock the lake. We just fish here.

themes.theme: Current market regime and AI debt issuance

insights.claim: Zimmerman sees today's setting as rhyming with the dot-com era: risk capital has flowed elsewhere, and ordinary assets are enormously mispriced on a sunny day with low VIX and ample liquidity, with less price discrimination than expected.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Low-vol complacency coexists with relative-value dislocations because capital is concentrated in a few themes.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are bringing about 250 billion of investment grade bonds, a size she compares with Treasury issuance, and are largely insensitive to basis points because they borrow as much, for as long, in whatever currency they can.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Price-insensitive supply from hyperscalers should widen spreads and create cross-currency and curve relative-value trades.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler data center tenants sign leases and guarantees that form a complex of mathematically related obligations across a small group of corporates, giving a rich relative-value surface.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: AI capex financing is creating structured, interlinked claims that can be mispriced.

insights.claim: Google's debut issuance included a hundred-year sterling bond, which Zimmerman calls not an easy set of cash flows to price or place.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Unusual maturities and currencies of AI-related debt create pricing gaps.

insights.claim: The long-standing marginal buyer of US bonds has been absent since QE ended: first Japanese, then Chinese buyers, then QE; the Treasury now plans buybacks and shortening of duration issuance, an era of policy experimentation she says is good for rates arbitrage.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: The absence of a natural buyer for duration raises odds of rates dislocations.

insights.claim: Because borrowers have to refinance debt issued in 2021-22 at higher rates, companies without a business model that supports rolling it face restructuring, and liability management exercises hinge on legal constraints and enforceability more than personalities.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Distressed credit outcomes will turn on contract rights and security interests, not just math.
insights.quote: If you're not at the table, you're on the menu

insights.claim: Zimmerman says endowments hold fewer bonds because bonds are no longer reliably anti-correlated with equities, and no one is sure borrowers will act in a balanced way in a downturn given the huge demand to borrow.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: The stock-bond hedge is questioned, which increases demand for uncorrelated alpha sources.

insights.claim: Bracebridge lent against ring-fenced property to a healthcare REIT that could borrow but not pay interest, borrowing at 8.5 and lending at 11.25, and hedged REIT survival by shorting another part of the capital structure.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Cross-team structured and corporate credit tie-ups can turn covenant constraints into secured, hedged high-carry loans.
insights.quote: borrowing at 8 and a half, you're lending to the same name at 11 and a quarter and you're secured on your long side

insights.claim: Zimmerman says Bracebridge's pricing question is whether a trade is true arbitrage with a catalyst and a defined exit via maturity or default, and compares each against what the firm earns for similar risk elsewhere on the platform.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Opportunities compete for capital on risk-adjusted return across the whole platform.

insights.claim: Single-name CDS, trading alongside deliverable bonds, let Bracebridge immunize corporate credit risk and price a capital stack, since default or payment probability must be the same at every level of the stack.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Capital-structure arbitrage relies on one coherent default probability across instruments.

insights.claim: Zimmerman says process plus people produces performance, and that curiosity is the trait that transcends all others in arbitrage investors.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Hiring for curiosity and rigor, then building process, is the stated organizing principle.
insights.quote: Process plus people is how you get performance.

insights.claim: Bracebridge aligns staff with investors by making employees investors, paying seniors more when investors do well, and rewarding the production of public goods such as models and methods.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Compensation tied to shared tools and investor outcomes sustains a long-tenured team.

insights.claim: Zimmerman's observation from Brown's investment committee is that people are not forward-looking, and that endowment choices are sometimes driven by what others do or previous commitments rather than price or risk-adjusted return.
insights.speaker: Nancy Zimmerman
insights.so_what: Institutional behavior is backward looking and path dependent, creating opportunities for the nimble.
